utterances.text: And I gathered these documents in a very serious way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was actually a very simple one. You were just asked to specify, to indicate, a time, a period, when you first started investigating these alleged war crimes. That was the question. And you said sometime around November, and I think you should have stopped there. Because otherwise we are never going to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, I started on the first day, as soon as I entered the building of the Court, and I entered on the 16th of October. It was on the 16th of October that I entered this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's your answer, and Madame Faveau will proceed to the next one, to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have my authority, Madame Faveau, just as I had given my authority to the Prosecutor on previous occasions, because sometimes it does happen that the witness not just the Judge, but all witnesses, go into tangents sometimes. If you think that is happening, you can just look at me. Either you do directly or ask for my intervention and I will do it. Because otherwise we'll never finish. Yes, Madame Faveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you started with the exhumations in the Sanski Most area. Was the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal involved in these exhumations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Office of the Prosecutor was involved in the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Madame Faveau, we had a document or two yesterday with the names even of the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you did this, in fact, but since when have you been cooperating with the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor of which Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this Tribunal. I apologise. Well, I can't give you a precise date right now, but I think I started cooperating immediately, as soon as I obtained the relevant documents, which we have examined here too. I immediately established contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the AID agency involved in the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the exhumation of the mass graves, no, it wasn't involved in them. Q, Did the AID agency ask you at a certain point not to provide the Office of the Prosecutor with the documents directly, but through the Agency?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I had gathered certain documents - and there were many such documents - I examined them and I even provided AID with some of the documents. I provided the AID in Bihac with all of the documents. So there are some documents which I haven't even managed to examine, but I personally took some of the documents to Bihac. I drove there in my own car and I submitted them to AID for the International Court. And I have a record of the documents that were submitted. And this is from Sanski Most. After the documents had been in my hands for a certain period of time, and after they had been examined by investigators from this Tribunal, AID asked me to provide them with the other documents, but I didn't want to do this, because it had been examined by the Tribunal and I still have these original documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally cooperate with AID?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there cooperation of any kind between you and AID?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The AID is a service, and it was my duty to send documents through the AID, to send documents to the Office of the Prosecutor of The Hague through the AID. This was the only means of sending documents. And in this sense, yes, I did cooperate with the AID, and the cooperation was correct. And similarly, AID officials would ask me, since I'm from Sanski Most and since I had also been in a camp and I knew people and I had information, they would sometimes ask me for certain information, and in that sense I did cooperate with the AID, if that's the kind of cooperation you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that the AID agency questions witnesses to find out information concerning the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just interrupt for one moment? And it's simply this, just to save time, if it helps. If Madame Faveau or Mr. Ackerman want to submit any matters for agreement on how AID and this office cooperate, then we're perfectly happy too deal with it rather than go through this tortuous process with the Judge, because it's self-evident. That AID takes statements because the Defence have these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would not involve Mr. Ackerman in this because he's not part of it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm just saying it may be a method of shortening this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And secondly, I think the witness has been asked a question, and if he -- it's a sort of a question that if he's familiar with the details, he can answer by either yes or no and that will be it and we can proceed, Ms. Korner. We actually all know what the answer is, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I mean. It's a bit -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Judge, you are requested to answer to this simple question: Is it exact to say that the AID agency questions witnesses to find out information concerning the war in Bosnia? Please answer -- if you know, please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally take statements from witnesses on behalf of AID?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of the AID, no, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do you think or do you propose you shouldn't answer this question? If need be, we can go into private session for a moment and you could perhaps explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to go into private session or are we going to continue like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suppose so. If there is a reason why the witness doesn't want to answer the question, he must give us a reason. So we go into private session for -- until necessary. Wait. When I tell you, please. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the question, Judge, is: Do you know someone called Zijad Ibric? And pardon me if I'm not pronouncing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next question, Madame Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this person work for the AID?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that in a case that came before this Tribunal, the Omarska case, were you informed that a statement which was taken by Zijad Ibric, that the authenticity of this statement had been questioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the basis of the objection, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The objection is: What happened in another case, whether there was objection taken to the authenticity, is irrelevant to this case unless there's some point of relevance shown that ties up with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But before that, there's even another matter, because if we're talking of a statement, that statement must be brought here and shown to the witness in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it is to be suggested to this witness that he was involved in the taking of a statement and there's going to be matters raised in this case about it, but we cannot possibly investigate what happened in another case in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner is right. What is your allegation? I mean, perhaps you can rephrase your question to Judge Draganovic, and if there is an allegation that you are making, then make it straight away. You have a right to put a direct question to him. In other words, if you are alleging that the witness was involved in the taking of a statement which was eventually contested as to its authenticity or whatever, you are perfectly entitled to put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wouldn't go that far, I'm afraid. She can put a statement to him saying was he involved in the taking of it and she can reopen the whole matter if indeed there was a discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can bring the statement to start with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, it's not a matter of simply contesting a statement; it's a matter of a graphological report that had been made. I tried to obtain this document, and apparently it disappeared, so I wasn't able to obtain it. It's apparently document D29/4 in the Omarska case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Omarska, you mean the Kvocka case, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know -- I'm sorry that Madame Faveau hasn't been able to obtain a report and we may be able to get it from our files, but she hasn't answered the question: What is the relevance to this witness of what may or may not have happened other case. And secondly, what may or may not have happened in another case is not admissible in the form in which she is trying to put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, there, but perhaps my problem is this, Ms. Korner: That as I read Madame Faveau, she thinks, or at least for her, this particular document exhibited or made use of and then contested in the Kvocka case is of some relevance, given this particular moment when this particular witness is giving evidence. So what I need from you, Madame Faveau, is to cross the Ts and put the dots on the Is and tell us what, if there is, is the involvement of the witness in relation to that particular document that the person that you mentioned earlier - I forgot his name now - yes, Ibric, allegedly compiled or took. And then we see after that how to go about it. But initially if you're going to ask the witness a question in relation to a document which is not before him, you have to be very specific and very precise. And also, we need to know whether he's aware of this statement, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think, before we go any further with this, it may be as well if the -- we may have the break, but to discuss this, because the witness is sitting here listening to this long discussion and it's really a matter of law as to whether Madame Faveau can proceed further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not just a matter of law. It's also a matter of questioning -- perhaps it's a simple question she can make.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to be very brief in order to bring this conversation to an end. Your Honours, you know that we have been contesting an entire series of documents from the AID. This witness at the request of the Prosecutor examined all the documents, most of which came from the AID, and it is only for this reason that I have asked him this question. In addition, this document is one of the Prosecutor's documents, and unfortunately I do not have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a document of the Prosecution in another case, not in this case. So what's the relevance of the question? I mean, perhaps you can ask the witness whether he has ever seen a statement made by or compiled by this other gentleman, provided there is some relevance of that statement to this case. If you merely are intending to attack the credibility of all the documentation originating from AID, that's a completely different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I object to. It goes back to what Mr. Ackerman was saying yesterday. Whether rightly or wrongly, the general sweeping allegation is being repeated that anything submitted by AID, prima facie, is a forgery unless they can prove the opposite. Now, that's fine. It's not a proper method to adopt. If there is a specific document that it is going to be suggested by either defendant to this witness that he knows something about it and that it is a forgery then fine let it be put, but a general sweeping statement that everything submitted by AID is, in our submission, not a proper way to cross-examine and not admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I think we need to take the half-hour break now. We'll resume at 1.00. In the meantime, think about it a little bit, because I think it's a case of either rephrasing your question or moving to the next question. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will go on to another question, but I will, however, try to explain what is it that I wanted to do. We are not challenging all the documents coming from AID simply because they come from AID, but there is a certain number that we do challenge because they have some other material defect, and the events at another trial confirm our opinion. So my opinion was quite simple: It was whether our witness is aware of the fact that some of the documents coming from AID have been brought into question. But I would like to now go into another issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd of April, during our hearing, you said that the ethnic communities had lived together in Sanski Most and that mixed marriages were quite numerous; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, first of all, I have been thinking about what you have been saying. I cannot concentrate on your question -- your statements that you just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget the statement. You've got nothing to do with it, Judge. Don't worry about it. Concentrate on this question that has just been put to you, and I will read out the question to you myself. Counsel has told you that on the 23rd of April, during our hearing, you said that the ethnic communities had lived together in Sanski Most and that mixed marriages were quite numerous, and she wants to know from you whether you stand by that statement, whether that statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there mixed marriages in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the same hearing on the 23rd of April, page 4853 of the French transcript, it is stated that you said that the Mahala, the population in Mahala, was 100 per cent Muslim. How can you then explain this statement of yours if the population was 100 per cent Muslim, how could there have been any mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking of mixed marriages, but now that you ask me if there were any mixed marriages in Mahala, I do know some Serb women who had married Muslims living in Mahala -- Bosniaks, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like the registrar to show the witness Exhibit P757.2, and I have to apologise to the Judges and to the Prosecution for not having included this document in my list. This is the map of the Sanski Most municipality, depicting the ethnic composition of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that the map indicates some data that are not completely correct. You said that there are some villages that are listed as being Serb villages, whereas they in fact were not Serb villages. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kasapnica is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it is not necessary for you to explain all this again. I just wanted to ask you if you still stand by what you have said earlier.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the way I said it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that goes for the village of Poljak too, which is indicated here as being a Croat village, and in your opinion it was a mixed population village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The map also shows, I think in the upper corner, the ethnic composition of the population as of 1995; is that correct? And it is also quite visible from the map that the majority of the population in 1995 was of Serb ethnic origin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that map, the ethnic composition of the population in the Sanski Most municipality in 1995 is shown, and if you look at the data shown there, you will see that the predominant majority of the population in Sanski Most municipality in 1995 was of Serb ethnic origin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was, until the 10th of October, 1995. So it's valid for 1995 until that date, when the BH army put -- or, in other words, when Sanski Most was liberated and when the Bosnia-Herzegovinian army entered Sanski Most. After that, the ethnic composition of the population changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether this map shows any specific date, or is it just dated 1995?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no date here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I ought to just remind everybody that this was produced by Mr. Inayat from the figures. It's not an official in that sense, document. That's all I'm saying. If there are any questions about its accuracy, Mr. Inayat will have to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. It's not an official map released --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not an official map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or like some of the others --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. It was an attempt to use a computer to demonstrate the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly what Ms. Korner has said, that would mean that this map is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all I'm saying is how this map was produced is something to ask Mr. Inayat what figures he used as opposed -- it's been given to the witness as a totally accurate depiction. It's -- I think Mr. Inayat is the best person to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think the witness has given a clear answer in the sense that after the 10th of October of 1995, the demographic situation changed. I mean, so we can have two maps, or two diagrams: One pre-10th October and one post-10th October we'll probably be contesting and fighting and arguing on that too. So let's proceed. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask a direct question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree with the fact that there are some inaccurate -- there is some inaccurate information contained in this map?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that. I can only say that there are some omissions that I pointed out here, and they concern the two villages that I mentioned. But we did specify that if the village of Kasapnica is joined by the village of Kljevci, then one could say that it was a Serb village, because it is quite close to it, because the Croat population had already left Kasapnica at an earlier date, and Poljak had a mixed population. It is hard to be very precise without the appropriate data, but I think in essence this map does reflect the situation as it was in, let's say, 1991, if we disregard the graphs here. They are valid for 1991, the ones for 1995 are also valid, but after October. We have to bear that in mind. But now the situation in Sanski Most is quite different, I mean the demographic situation. So the map can be used, and any errors are minor. And I, after all, explained them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs did you find in Sanski Most upon your return in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but there were a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd of April, during our hearing, you spoke about the constituencies in Bosnia. You said that there were seven constituencies, one of which was Banja Luka. The constituencies, did they correspond to the communities of municipalities that are associations of municipalities that existed at the time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regions, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of these regions was the Banja Luka region; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you had not received your salary from the month of February onwards. Your colleague Serbs, did they receive any salaries?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started receiving their salaries as soon as we were expelled from the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between February and May 1992, did your Serb colleagues receive their salaries in that period?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the treatment was the same for everyone as regards the salaries?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the registrar to show the witness the Exhibit 700. I think that on page 3 of that document there is a pamphlet entitled "Dear Brother Serbs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found this document? Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At our hearing on the 24th of April, you described this leaflet as an act of Serbian propaganda; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this document was found?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, this document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the exact location where the document was found?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the premises of the Serbian Democratic Party, but I may be wrong on this account. But at any rate, I do have its original in my office in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who found this document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at this document, would you agree with me that this document was written in the Ijekavian dialect?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you purport to say that Serbs did not use the Ijekavian dialect and that they didn't use the Roman alphabet in writing? Well, that's my answer to you, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think anything, I don't purport to say anything; I'm merely and asking you whether this document was written in the Ijekavian dialect, that's all?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's written in the Ijekavian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd of April you were telling us about the members of the 6th Brigade who were fighting in Croatia, and you stated that while they fought in Croatia, that their companies paid them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The war in Croatia happened in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Bosnia, in 1991, was still a part of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 6th Brigade was a brigade that was a part of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the JNA was the Yugoslav army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Croats and Muslims that responded to the call-up in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the call-up -- the call for the mobilisation. Let me say this: The 6th Krajina Brigade was a unit, a brigade whose composition corresponded to the ethnic composition of the population. So people got the call-up papers and they responded. However, as far as I know - and you have to take into account that I'm not a military expert. I did not really deal with this issue in detail, but I lived in the city, in the town, and I was also a conscript. I had my own military assignment. So I knew something about it. When people had to go to the theatres of operation in Croatia, to be more specific, in Titova Korenica, I think that people deserted en masse, conscripts of Croat and Bosniak ethnic background deserted en masse. I don't know of anyone remaining in the brigade, apart from one officer, who was in Croatia, in the theatre of war there. He was a Bosniak. I don't know of anyone else. So what I know is this people abandoned the unit en masse, people returned their weapons and equipment to the command of the 6th Krajina Brigade, and they returned all the equipment that it had. As I have already said, I'm not really an expert for these military matters and it happened a long time ago, so I've now told you all that I can remember about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that you just spoke about, that Croat or Bosniak who remained in the army, was he a professional soldier or was it a mobilised person who otherwise was employed in another company?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a reserve officer. He was in the engineers. So he was in the theatre of war in Croatia. He was engaged on bridge and road construction, or perhaps demolition. I don't know. I mean, he himself probably knows what he was doing. I know that he spent the rest -- throughout the period of the war, he was in Serbia, and he returned to Sanski Most recently. I don't know about the others. I think that the people deserted en masse in 1991. I know a lot of people - my friends, officers, reserve officers and soldiers, and in 1992 they had problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to that person, the Croat or the Bosniak who went to fight in Croatia. Can you tell me: Was he employed in a company in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as I can remember, he had his own private business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that quite a few Bosniaks and Croats deserted, that virtually all of them deserted. You also said that in 1992 people began to be fired from their jobs in Sanski Most. Does it mean that no measures were taken against the persons who deserted in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that any measures were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a judge. Do you agree with the statement that according to the Yugoslav law, failure to respond to the call-up is a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that in this specific case it was a criminal offence. It was not a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, was the federal Penal Code still in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was still in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not correct that Article 214 of that Act foresees punishment for the failure to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did stipulate such punishment. I wouldn't now go into the reasons which lead me not to think that it's a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do agree that the Federal Penal Code provided that this anticipate act was an illicit act and that this act was sanctioned? I'm talking about the failure to respond to mobilisation. I'm not talking about any specific cases.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You insist on me speaking about this. Please, spare me, because if you force someone to go to war to fight against people in Croatia, then if a person deserts, that is no crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your interpretation, but I'm going to move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. That would be better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned terrorist acts that had been committed against the Croatian population. Do you remember speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you yourself went to the site of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spoke about the debris of these explosive devices, including rifle-launched grenades; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did your military service. Could you explain to us how rifle-launched grenades are used exactly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me how they are used? You use a rifle, a semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. My question wasn't how they were used, but for what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question was translated -- your question, Madame Faveau, could be an interpretation error. I don't know. But your question was: Could you explain to us how rifle-launched grenades are used exactly? So if that's not the question that you are asking -- now you're asking --

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that -- what I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What they are used for?

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why would one resort to rifle-launched grenade and not a hand-launched grenade? I would imagine, because I'm not a military man, I know nothing about the subject. Perhaps you could enlighten us, if you know. If you don't know, just say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could be more precise, it concerns an explosive device which is launched in this manner?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This grenade is put on a semi-automatic rifle and it's fired from this rifle. In the Kruhare settlement, where there are Croatian houses too, I went there to carry out an investigation. Two rifle-launched grenades had been fired there from a precise point, from a certain house, and they had been fired in the direction of a certain house. We found traces on the entrance to the house. One the of grenades had exploded and one grenade had not exploded, if I am precise. That is one investigation. If necessary, I can mention others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it may be our fault because we are not being very precise. What the question really is: Why would one want to use a rifle-launched grenade and not some other kind of grenade? What's the advantage of using a rifle-launched grenade? What's so characteristic, what's so important, what's so advantageous about this kind of grenade, or the method of launching such a grenade? Is it because it reaches further? I don't know. I mean, I don't know anything about the subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you don't know, say "I don't know" and leave it at that. If she had asked me the question, I would have told you, Madame Faveau, find someone else, because I don't know how to answer -- I don't know the answer to that. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Madame Faveau is moving to other subject, there's a matter I want to raise before the end of this session which has arisen. If she is still going on, that's fine, but if not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also there was something else I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still haven't got my answer. I shall put the question another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the damage caused by this rifle-launched grenade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree if I said that rifle-launched grenades don't leave very important -- don't cause very important damage to houses and that they have a different purpose?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kill. They explode and they kill.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question about this subject and then I will stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were able to establish that this debris was as a result of -- that this debris came from the military factory in Bugojno. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the explosions of certain bombs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not all the debris came from this factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put that question a little more precisely? Could you reformulate it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the debris that you found, did all the debris come from the Bugojno factory?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of some explosions, I went to carry out an on-site investigation, in cases where hand grenades had been thrown, so there is certain information about this. And on several occasions, in several cases, I was able to determine that the hand grenades were of military origin. They came from the military factory in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be better if I stopped now, because I'm not going to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Faveau. We will continue with your evidence on Tuesday morning, not Monday, for a very simple reason you may have been told already, that Monday is a feast day, a public holiday here, and we won't be working.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a piece of information that might be of use. I think that, unfortunately, I will need an entire session on Tuesday. This might be useful information for Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, unfortunately it's too late to stop the witness coming. He's arriving this weekend. It can't be helped. I'm sure that Defence counsel will help us out with VWS, who are likely to shoot us, but that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness can leave, Your Honour. The matter I want to raise doesn't affect him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. See you again on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's what Madame Faveau said at the beginning of the session, that on behalf of General Talic they're not challenging all the documents coming from AID, simply because they come from AID, but there are a number we do challenge because they are false. If that is right, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't look at the transcript. If that's what it says in the transcript, that's not what I said. I said that we contest a certain number of documents from the AID. If there are other defects, material defects in them. That's what I said. That is to say, there is no signature, no stamp, no date, no number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's completely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From what I heard as well. I take your word, Madame Faveau. I don't even doubt that for a moment. But I fail to understand how what you said just now was translated or interpreted as meaning amount to forgeries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I wouldn't have trouble then, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can leave it, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. There is a point to be made. I'm sorry, Your Honour. That if there is a suggestion, and I think there must be, because otherwise the line of cross-examination doesn't make sense either, that certain documents that we have produced in this case are forgeries of some kind or another, in other words, that they are not what they purport to be on their face, then I think that these documents must be put to this witness, or a witness, and not just the general allegation. Because this witness is in a clear position to deal with originals. Your Honour will recall that one of the matters that he was asked about, he said they come from a book which is still in Sanski Most. So, Your Honour, my only -- all I'm saying is if there are going to be -- if the Defence are going to be saying that documents we have produced from Sanski Most are from evidence they have, or instructions, whatever it may be, forgeries, then that ought to be put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I recall well that this question arose in the very first week of our labours here in this case, because there was an allegation that there were some forgeries. That much I remember very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember how we dealt with it, what was said beyond that, because more or less the whole admissibility aspect in a very broad manner, admitting everything and then reserving the position of the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were sweeping assertions made that documents that come from AID, on the face of it, could be forgeries and weren't to be trusted. That's fine. It's not fine, because I've already objected to that. But if there are specified documents which it's going to be suggested at some stage are in fact forgeries and there is a witness there who is able to deal with the provenance of those documents, then it's my submission that that should be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to reassure you and to reassure Ms. Korner, this seems obvious to me, but unfortunately I've already started my cross-examination. I've only been cross-examining for one hour so I haven't had time to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing I wanted to raise myself is very simple. I met this morning with one of my legal assistants who is working on the redaction of the decision on Rule 70. I would prefer if you will agree that she approaches you by handing you a draft of what she is suggesting ought to be redacted. Because I would feel more comfortable when we discuss this if we already have an indication from you that you agree with the proposed redactions. For example -- anyway, I have asked her to mark the decision and approach you, and then please feed her back as to -- and if we need to discuss it, then we discuss it; if we don't need to discuss it -- I don't think there should be much controversy. But there are some suggestions we she has made which in my opinion I would rather hear what you have to say. Because if they don't need to be redacted, they won't be redacted. If they need to be redacted -- for example, if one of the accused filed motion confidentially or something like that. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The major force of my motion, Your Honour, was just to try to reduce it to the pure legal findings and decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you're probably going to agree with what she suggests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the humanitarian organisation in my mind, at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, finally, I gave to the Defence yesterday and to Your Honours a copy of the proposed redaction for the one Rule 92 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. I'm not talking about that. I'm not talking about that, I'm talking about the 70 one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know but I thought we finished with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've had no feedback from either the Court or the Defence as to whether that's a suitable redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I just -- it's taken her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a disadvantage of being -- finding yourself behind Mr. Ackerman. She was on her feet before you were, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. IVANOVIC-FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that I will make life easier for you, because I agree with everything that has been done, not because I agree but because I know that my position -- the position I'm in is not acceptable, because our position is that this story that has to do with Rule 70 and the witness who was brought here, this should all be made public for several reasons, because I know that this isn't possible, I will accept any redactions that the legal officer might make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to the 92 bis, and we should be out of here, but with regard to the 92 bis, I just need a little bit of time. It took the Prosecution a long time to redact it. I'd like a few minutes to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we adjourn until Monday -- until Tuesday, sorry, we won't bring you here Monday. My apologies to the interpreters and the technicians for keeping you here beyond the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
